title: Nautical Bearing Calculator: Course and Miles
description: Compute the initial bearing and nautical distance between two points with the Nautical Bearing Calculator — course and miles for the chart. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, New York to Boston opens at an initial bearing of 052° and runs 165.3 nautical miles — a coastal hop — while New York to London opens at 051° yet runs 2,991 nautical miles of Atlantic.
quick_answer: The Nautical Bearing Calculator computes the initial great-circle bearing and the distance in nautical miles between two coordinate points. Enter the pair and read the departure course and the sea miles to run — a passage plan's first two numbers.

body.t: Leg by leg, harbour to harbour: initial bearing plus sea miles per leg is the skeleton a full plan hangs courses, ETAs and fuel on. Times come from the
Navigation students check hand-plotted courses against the computed truth — the bearing should match to the degree, and where it does not, the plot learns something.
Open-water crossings of bays and sounds are bearing problems with consequences. A computed course plus a compass beats a guess plus optimism.
The same great-circle maths serves VFR planning — initial course and nautical distance are aviation's native pair too.

From New York, Boston and London both open near 051–052° — the great circle's indifference to your ambitions. Distance separates them: 165.3 nm up the coast, 2,991.4 nm across the ocean (JFK–LHR). Same first course, different voyages entirely.

A great-circle course changes as you sail it: the New York–London initial bearing of 051° at departure becomes a different arrival bearing, because the shortest path curves across the chart's rhumb lines. Steering one fixed compass course draws the longer rhumb line instead — the distinction this calculator is precise about.

faq: Initial great-circle bearing — the shortest path's departure course, which then evolves. Constant-bearing rhumb lines are the alternative geometry, with their own tools in the bearing family; mixing the two mid-passage is how landfalls get missed.
Why is the return bearing not exactly opposite?

On a sphere, the great circle's direction at London toward New York (288°) is not the departure bearing plus 180 (231°) — convergence of the meridians twists it. Both numbers are computed fresh for each direction.
True. Apply your chart's compass rose (declination/variation) and your vessel's deviation to get the course you actually steer — the calculator stays in the true frame all chartwork starts from.
Great-circle on a spherical Earth — within a fraction of a percent of the ellipsoidal truth, far inside any passage plan's weather margin. The coordinates' quality is the real limit.
Not in a bearing: this is geometry between two points. Real tracks respect separation schemes, hazards and weather — the plan layers those over the computed skeleton.
Yes — each waypoint pair is a leg with its own opening bearing and miles. The plan is the chain; this calculator forges the links.
The distance also reads in kilometres and statute miles — but the nautical mile's kinship with latitude (one minute of arc) is why the sea keeps it, and why this page leads with it.
